activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
Victor had been trying to figure out the new kid all afternoon, and the new kid was not helping. Cyrus had come to Ayesha's house with a battered suitcase full of photos: a flat in Cairo, a school in Manila, a street market in Kuala Lumpur, an apartment in Toronto. Four cities, four countries, and he could name them all.

"Okay, so where are you from?" Victor asked, pointing at the Toronto picture, because that was the most recent one.

Cyrus shuffled the photos instead of answering. Ayesha's little brother kept leaning over the table and obstructing Victor's view of the pile, so Victor pulled the photos closer and dealt them out like cards, one city in front of Cyrus at a time.

"Pick one," Victor said. "That's the test. Whichever one you pick first, that's where you're from."

"That's a bad test," Ayesha said. "I'm from here, and I'd still hesitate. My parents are from Lagos." She held up a hand when Victor opened his mouth. "But I'm not from Lagos. See the problem?"

Cyrus laughed for the first time all afternoon. "It's a paradox," he said. "Every answer I give is true and wrong at the same time. My parents are from one place, I grew up in other places, and now we're here. If someone asks where I'm from, the honest answer takes ten minutes."

Victor had a theory forming, something half remembered from a book his mother left on the kitchen counter. He pulled out his phone and searched: children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture. The words came up fast, and he read the name twice to be sure.

"There's a name for you," Victor said. "Third culture kid. Some American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, came up with it back in the 1950s."

"Say it again," Cyrus said.

"Third culture kid."

Cyris repeated it quietly, then wrote it on the back of the Cairo photo. "Next time someone asks, I'll say that first, then take my ten minutes."

"Perfect," Ayesha said. "Now we just have to teach the whole school the phrase."

Victor grinned and gathered up the cards. "Deal them out again. This time I get to guess which country is next."

"Toronto," Cyrus said. "It was inevitable."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: A kneaded eraser can be pressed and shaped to lift graphite off the paper, which lets an artist pull a highlight back out of shading.
story:
Stella had decided that her pencil was a wand and her paper was a small planet. The planet was perfectly round, because Ms. Tse had set a wooden ball on the picnic table and told the art shed kids to make it look like it was sitting in real light. "Find the highlight," Ms. Tse had said, "the brightest spot where the lamp hits it. Then let the shadow curl around the far side, and let the sphere drop a cast shadow onto the table, like a dark puddle." Stella loved the idea of a puddle made of darkness. She was halfway to making a planet so real that astronauts would want to land on it when her pencil slipped.

Donovan, who was drawing a sphere that looked more like a potato, leaned over. "You just scribbled right across your bright part. The planet has a storm now."

"It's not a storm, it's a disaster." Stella stared at the smudged patch where the highlight should have been, the one place that needed to stay white and glowing. If she shaded harder everywhere else, the spot would still be gray, like a dirty moon. She could not retrieve the whiteness by drawing. Whiteness was the one thing a pencil could not make.

Then she remembered the gray lump in her pencil case, the soft, squishy eraser Ms. Tse had handed out that looked like a piece of dough. It was called a kneaded eraser, and it did not rub like a normal eraser. Stella pressed it flat between her fingers, shaped the edge into a small point, and touched it gently to the gray patch. When she lifted it, some of the graphite had sunk into the eraser, and the paper underneath was paler. She dabbed again. And again. Each press lifted a little more, and slowly the highlight bloomed back out of the darkness like a window opening on the far side of space.

"It's eating the shading," she whispered. "It's like a creature that eats shadow." She rolled the gray-stained eraser in her palm, thinking of the artisan who must have invented it, some old craftsperson in a workshop who wanted to pull light back out of a drawing the way you pull a rope out of a well. She began testing the limits. A flat press lifted a wide, soft band, good for a gentle glow. A pinched point retrieved a single tiny star of white. She could even curve the shadow's edge by pressing along a line parallel to the sphere's round side.

Kayden wandered over from the pottery wheel with clay on her elbows. "How did you get that to glow?"

Stella held up the eraser, now marbleized with gray streaks like a tiny planet of its own. "Shadow-eating space dough," she said, and pressed it once more against the cast shadow's edge, watching the dark puddle shrink back toward the wooden ball.

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: A large U.S. survey of teens aged 13 to 18 found that about a third had had an anxiety disorder at some point, the most common kind of mental disorder among them.
story:
Naomi had been counting Taha's "I can'ts" all week, and by Wednesday morning at canoe camp the count was up to eleven. He wouldn't get in the boat on Monday, wouldn't eat at the long table on Tuesday, and today he was sitting on the dock with his knees pulled up while everyone else raced to the water. She flopped down beside him, sandals slapping the boards.

"I made a chart," she announced, unfolding a page from her notebook. "Eleven times since Sunday. And here's the thing, it's not random. It spikes before group stuff and drops when it's just us. That's a pattern." She loved patterns. Patterns meant you could categorize things, file them like the insect cases at the nature hut, and once you filed something you could do something about it.

"So what's the category?" Taha asked, staring at the lake like it might stare back.

"That's what I'm figuring out. Ms. Rao keeps a poster in the first aid cabin. I bet there's a formula for this, like, signs plus a grown-up you trust equals help."

She ran up the hill to the cabin, and Ms. Rao listened, then pulled a binder off the shelf and flipped to a page. "Look at this," she said. "A big U.S. survey of teenagers, thirteen to eighteen, found about a third of them had an anxiety disorder at some point. Most common mental disorder among them."

"A third?" Naomi said. She did the math fast. If there were thirty-six campers, that could be twelve kids. Taha wasn't some strange category nobody had seen before. He was practically ordinary math. She grinned all the way back down the hill.

"Guess what," she said, dropping onto the dock. "You're not rare. A third of teens in this whole huge survey had anxiety. And Ms. Rao says talking to her counts as a plan, not as tattling."

Taha looked at her, then at the water. Then came the twist: he pulled a crumpled page from his pocket, his own chart, her name at the top. "I've been counting your worry signs too," he said. "Nine. You grind your teeth before every swim test."

Naomi laughed so hard she nearly rolled off the dock. "Then let's be competent together. We tell Ms. Rao at lunch, both charts."

"Deal," Taha said, and stuck out his hand to shake.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: US food safety agencies advise keeping a refrigerator at 4 degrees Celsius, or 40 degrees Fahrenheit, or colder.
story:
The driving school smelled like burnt coffee and old carpet, and Aubrey sat in the corner doing homework while her dad practiced parallel parking in the lot outside. Mr. Sow, the owner, drank milk in his coffee all day, and because the corner store was only two blocks away, he had started sending Aubrey for a carton each morning. "My first solo mission," she told him, and she liked counting the change into his palm, nickel by nickel, until the numbers matched.

The third carton turned sour after only a day, and the fourth one too. Aubrey refused to resign herself to sour coffee. The store's milk couldn't be bad, because Jessie, who worked the register, said the delivery truck came every morning and the cold case hummed all night. That left one suspect: the little fridge under Mr. Sow's desk. There was a contradiction in it somehow, she thought, a machine made for cold that was letting milk spoil. She borrowed Jessie's cooking thermometer from the store, the kind with the long metal spike, and slid it into a glass of water on the fridge shelf.

"Forty-nine," she read aloud, frowning. She turned the dial one number colder and came back an hour later, hands still cold from walking the two blocks in the wind. Forty-two. She turned it again. Brynlee, waiting for her own ride home from the driving school, watched over her shoulder. "Forty," Aubrey announced the next hour, holding up the thermometer like a prize.

Mr. Sow squinted at the little line on the dial. "My last teacher put a sticker here," he said. "Keeps it at 40 degrees Fahrenheit, 4 Celsius, or colder. I thought that was just decoration."

"So does the milk," said Aubrey, and she set the fresh carton on the shelf, right beside the sticker.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: Borrowing 100 dollars at 20 percent yearly interest and repaying it after one year costs about 20 dollars in interest, or more if interest compounds.
story:
Victor counted the crumpled bills in the shoebox for the third time that afternoon, as if the total might change out of pure stubbornness. Forty-two dollars. The bike at Miller's Sports cost one hundred and sixty, and every Saturday he and Rafael sold lemonade from the folding table on Ms. Chatterjee's corner, earning about ten dollars a week. At that rate, summer would end before the shoebox did. "You should just put it on your mom's card," Rafael said, stirring the pitcher with a wooden spoon. "She said you could, right?"

Victor's mother had said it exactly one week ago, standing in the kitchen with a card in her hand. She would charge the bike now, and Victor would pay her back a little each week from the stand. It had sounded wonderful then, so wonderful that he'd almost run to the store that same night. But something Rafael's cousin had said kept circling back to him: borrowed money isn't free, because a card charges interest. Victor didn't know what that meant in real dollars, and it bothered him the way an itch behind the elbow bothers you, invisible but definitely there.

He worked it out on the back of a napkin while Rafael poured. "If I borrow a hundred dollars at twenty percent interest a year, and I pay it back after one whole year, that's about twenty dollars extra. A hundred borrowed costs me around a hundred and twenty." Rafael squinted at the napkin. "So the bike doesn't cost one sixty. It costs one eighty." Victor nodded slowly. "And my mom said it could be more than twenty, something about interest building on interest. She called it compounding." A cold drop of condensation slid off the pitcher and soaked through the napkin's corner, blurring nothing important, because the numbers were already burned into his head.

Emrik biked past just then, ringing his bell twice, and the sound of it settled the argument before Victor even admitted he was having one. He watched Emrik coast down the hill, wind in his shirt, and remembered how he'd felt a week ago, certain that waiting was for patient people and he was not one of them. Now the waiting felt different. Twenty dollars was two whole Saturdays of lemonade, sticky hands and all, handed over for nothing. A spontaneous plan rose in him, fully formed: he would keep selling, save the full amount, and own the bike outright.

Ms. Chatterjee came out with a plate of biscuits for the boys and stayed to watch a parliament of starlings land noisily in her maple tree, dozens of them chattering and rearranging themselves like a committee that couldn't agree. "You're not charging the bike anymore," she observed, dipping a biscuit in her tea. "I changed my mind," Victor said. "Borrowing costs more than it looks. I'm saving first."

She smiled and didn't say whether she thought that was wise or merely slow, and Victor found he didn't need her to. He taped the napkin inside the shoebox lid, right above the money, and poured Rafael a cup of lemonade with ice.

"First customer of the rest of the summer," Rafael said, clinking his paper cup against Victor's.

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: In the decimal coordinates used by GPS and online maps, latitudes south of the equator and longitudes west of the prime meridian are written as negative numbers.
story:
The GeoClub challenge ended at three o'clock, and Aubrey had exactly one lunch period left to find Lima, Buenos Aires and Sydney on the giant world map outside Mr. Nair's room. Whoever pinned all three cities first won the atlas. Tommy had already pinned Lima. Grady had pinned Lima and Buenos Aires and was squinting at his slip of paper for the third.

Aubrey unrolled her coordinates. "Buenos Aires. 34.6 south, 58.4 west," she read, and typed the numbers into the old laptop Mr. Nair kept on the cart beside the map. The online map loaded slowly, the way it always did, and then it showed a pin in the middle of a green landmass with tiny roads winding through it. It looked nothing like Argentina. Grady leaned over her shoulder.

"Your pin precedes your city by a whole ocean," he said. "That's not even the right continent."

Tommy laughed, then stopped when he saw Aubrey's face. "Hey, you'll still get it," he said, and slid his own slip across the cart so she could compare. His coordinates for Lima ended with "12.0 south, 77.0 west," and when he typed his, the map showed a coastal city with the Pacific right where it should be. His numbers were positive on the screen, with tiny minus signs in front. Aubrey's did not have them.

She looked at her slip again. She had written 34.6 and 58.4, both positive, because that was how she thought of numbers on a map. But Tommy typed his as negative. So the map must treat south and west as negative numbers, at least in the decimal coordinates it used. That was her idea, and it was testable. She deleted her pin and typed minus 34.6 and minus 58.4. The screen zoomed to a wide river, blocks of buildings, a coastline. Buenos Aires.

"That's it," Aubrey said. "South of the equator and west of the prime meridian. You have to type the minus sign or the map lands on the other side of the world."

"Then Sydney's going to be easy," said Tommy. "It's east, so it stays positive, and it's south, so it doesn't."

They ran through the possibilities together, because Grady was still stuck and the clock above the door showed twelve minutes left. Sydney, minus 33.8 and positive 151.2, appeared on the first try. Grady found Buenos Aires with Aubrey's rule and pinned it with two minutes to spare. On the wall above the map hung a poster from science class about rainforest food chains, and Aubrey pointed at the word decomposer printed beside a drawing of mushrooms. "That poster comes in second place," she said. "Today the minus sign is the most powerful little thing in this hallway."

At three o'clock, Mr. Nair counted three pins in each city and handed Aubrey the atlas, warm from sitting on the sunny shelf. Grady held the door, and Tommy said, "Same time next month?" Aubrey tucked the atlas under her arm and said, "Bring your minus signs."

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun; the phases show how much of that lit half faces Earth.
story:
Grandpa's reading lamp was the brightest thing in the den, so Autumn unplugged it, carried it to the middle of the rug, and clamped the shade so it pointed sideways. Cassia held the orange Nerf ball while Autumn read the assignment sheet aloud. "Mandatory project: demonstrate the phases of the Moon. Anyone who forgets has to enroll in the make-up session Saturday morning."

"Which is basically prison," Cassia said. "Turn on the lamp."

Autumn clicked it on. "You be the Moon. Walk around me." Cassia orbited slowly, holding the ball at arm's length, while Autumn, playing Earth, watched the light slide across the orange surface. Halfway around, the ball showed a fat curve of light like a sideways smile. "That's a crescent," Autumn said. "See? Only a sliver lit."

"No," Cassia said, and Autumn frowned, because Cassia was supposed to be the agreeable one. "The whole half facing the lamp is lit. It's just turned away from you. Come here and look from my side."

Autumn crossed the rug and stood where the lamp stood. The whole lit half of the ball glared back at her, bright and round. She walked back to Earth's spot. Sliver. Back to the lamp. Whole lit half, every time. "Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun," she said slowly, "even when it looks like a crescent from Earth. The phases just show how much of that lit half is facing us." She grabbed her notebook and wrote it down before the idea could escape.

A knock came at the screen door, and Mr. Sow from next door leaned in, squinting at the lamp. "Everything all right in here? Looks like a landing pad."

"We're doing science," Cassia said. "The lamp is the Sun. I'm the Moon. Autumn's Earth."

"Then Earth's wearing one sock and a hoodie inside out," said Mr. Sow.

Autumn looked down, laughed, and kept orbiting the lamp with her pencil tucked behind her ear. "Half of you is always lit," she told Cassia grandly. "Even the parts that look dark."

"I'd rather be the adversary," Cassia said. "The Moon never gets to talk."

Autumn circled her one more time, watching the sliver grow into a half, then a whole glowing face, and held out her hand for the ball. "My turn to orbit."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The bus hadn't left the parking lot yet, and Logan was already holding his phone above the seat like a trophy. "Told you," he said. "Rankings don't lie. Montero is tenth in the league. Tenth. That means nine whole quarterbacks are better."

Ella squinted at the screen. Behind the big ranking number there was a whole wall of smaller ones: completions, attempts, yards, touchdowns, interceptions. "Tenth in what, exactly?" she asked.

"In quarterback rating," Logan said, as if that settled it. "It's one number. One. That's the beauty of it."

Jana leaned over from the seat across the aisle. "One number for a whole season of games? That seems like a lot of squishing."

Eella couldn't stop thinking about it as the bus lurched out of the lot. A season was hundreds of throws. Some were beautiful spirals into tight windows, some were dump-offs where the running back did all the work, some were dropped by receivers who couldn't catch a cold. All of that, mashed together and squeezed out as one number. She was optimistic that she could find the squishing machine somewhere online, but she didn't have service on the bus, so she'd have to wait, which was its own kind of torture.

By the time they reached her street, she had a plan. "Logan," she said, standing in the aisle, "if one number can rank a whole season, how would you rank one game? Like, what's the best a quarterback could possibly do?"

Logan shrugged. "A hundred. Perfect score is always a hundred. Everybody knows that."

"That's what I thought too," Ella said, and she anticipated his face going through three stages: confident, confused, annoyed. "My cousin had a game on yesterday, and the announcer said a perfect passer rating is 158.3."

Jana burst out laughing. "A perfect score of 158.3? Who picked that?"

"The announcer said the passer rating combines a bunch of passing stats into one number," Ella went on, "and it goes from zero up to a maximum of 158.3. So it's not out of a hundred. Montero's rating isn't like a grade on a math test."

Logan looked at his phone again, then at her, then at his phone. "So when they show the one big number..."

"A lot of little numbers, wearing a trench coat," Jana said.

At her front door that afternoon, Ella looked it up before she even took off her backpack. The little numbers were all still there, underneath, like the bus wheels under all those kids. She texted Logan a screenshot and one line: "Your tenth-best quarterback, in six parts."

Her phone buzzed almost immediately. "Fine. But he's still tenth."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil that producers use again.
story:
Naomi crouched in the corner of Ms. Littlechild's farm, holding her notebook so tightly that the edges dug into her palm. The assignment was due tomorrow: draw a food chain that started with the sun and ended with a top predator, then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. Everyone else had finished theirs in class. Mitchell had drawn grass, a rabbit, and a hawk in about ten minutes and then gone outside to help unload hay. Naomi had written the sun, then clover, then a rabbit, then an owl, because Ms. Littlechild had pointed out the owl box on the barn and said a nocturnal hunter lived there, hunting in the dark while the farm slept.

But when Naomi tested her chain the way the assignment asked, something went wrong. She imagined the clover vanishing, and the rabbits going hungry, and the owl losing its prey; that part made sense. Then she flipped the problem around. If the rabbits ceased to exist, what would happen to the clover? Nothing in her drawing fed the clover except the sun, and she had a sinking feeling that sunlight alone was not the whole answer. She had watched her mother's houseplant wilt in poor soil even by a bright window. Something had to reach the clover from the soil, something invisible, and she could not draw what she could not name.

She walked the fence line with Mitchell, peering under bushes. "I need to see where old plants go," she said, and he shrugged and led her past the compost bins to a shady patch behind the barn. There, on a rotting log half sunk in the leaves, grew a cluster of pale mushrooms. Naomi knelt down. The log was soft and crumbly where the mushrooms touched it, as though something were quietly taking it apart. She poked the wood with a stick and it flaked away into dark, rich crumbs that looked exactly like the good soil in the garden beds.

"Mushrooms are fungi," Mitchell said, reading over her shoulder as she flipped through the battered field guide in the barn. "It says right here they break down dead plants and animals and return the nutrients to the soil." Naomi stared at the page while her pulse hammered. There it was, the missing link, the hidden one that ran backward, from the dead to the living, feeding the clover from below. On the walk back she tried one more test in her head: no fungi, no breaking down, no nutrients going back, and the soil would slowly run out of what the clover needed.

That evening she redrew the chain with a looping arrow beneath it, from the owl and rabbit and clover down to the mushrooms, and back up to the soil and the clover again. The suspense of the blank page was gone. When Ms. Littlechild looked it over the next morning, she tapped the loop with one finger and smiled. "Everyone forgets that one," she said. "What do you call them?" Naomi set her pencil down on the drawing, point resting on the mushrooms. "Decomposers," she said.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: The equilibrium price is the price at which the amount buyers want to buy equals the amount sellers want to sell.
story:
Naomi dragged the folding table into the driveway and propped up the cardboard sign her dad had helped her letter: STRAWBERRIES, $5 A PINT. She had spent her birthday money on four crates of berries from the farm stand by the highway, because Mr. Krause had provoked a question she couldn't shake. "Ask me why strawberries cost more in winter," he had said at the bus stop, and she had been chewing on it ever since.

Jayden arrived first, then Kaliyah with a coin purse and a plan. "Five dollars is too much," Kaliyah said, pointing at the sign. "My mom gets them cheaper at the store." Naomi argued back, but the first half hour proved Kaliyah right. Three customers walked past without stopping, and one man laughed out loud, which Naomi felt was rude and also possibly fair.

She flipped the cardboard over and wrote $2. That worked almost too well. Two women bought six pints between them, a jogger bought two, and by three o'clock only five pints remained with a whole hour of selling left. Naomi sat on the curb and made her inference out loud. "Two dollars made people want way more than we had. Five dollars made them want way less. Somewhere in between there's a price where what people want to buy is exactly what we want to sell." Kaliyah squinted at her. "Like, sell out right at closing time?" "Exactly at closing time," Naomi said, and wrote $3 on a fresh sign.

At $3, it wasn't instant. A boy on a scooter bought one pint, then circled back for another. Kaliyah added a sample dish, because she noticed a shy little girl staring at the berries without asking, and gave her the biggest strawberry on top. Naomi thought that was better business than any sign. By 3:55, one pint sat alone in the shade. "Lower it?" Jayden suggested. Naomi changed her mind about holding firm and crossed out the 3 to make it 2. "One pint, two dollars," she called, "last of the day." A woman in a garden hat turned around and came back with her wallet just as the clock hit four.

That night Naomi wrote a message on the fridge whiteboard, in her best printing: "TO TEAM BERRY: We found the price where buyers want to buy exactly as much as sellers want to sell. Mr. Krause says that is the equilibrium price. It was $3. Next weekend: lemonade?" Kaliyah had already texted back before Naomi even put the marker down. "Lemonade. But I'm in charge of samples."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
The basket handle was a smooth orange polymer, and Aaron carried it through the sliding doors behind his mother, straight into a crowd that was thicker than usual for a Tuesday. His little sister had been up all night with a fever, and his mother had written a list: children's fever medicine, popsicles, tissues. On the way to the pharmacy aisle they passed a tower of strawberry boxes stacked so high it looked like it might tip over, each one marked with a big red tag. Two dollars, down from five.

"Whoa," said Aaron. "Why so cheap?"

"There's too many of them," said Theo, who had tagged along with his own mother and was now trailing Aaron like a second shadow. "My uncle grows them and he won't stop talking about it. Everybody's flooded with berries."

At the medicine aisle, the shelf was nearly bare. Three boxes of children's fever reducer stood alone at the back, and the price sticker read twelve dollars. Aaron remembered it costing six, because he had bought some for his mother in the spring when she had the flu.

"That doubled," he said.

A woman in front of them reached for a box anyway, checked the price, and put it in her basket without a pause. Then an older man did the same with the last adult cold medicine. Behind him, Ms. Shin from next door stood squinting at the shelf with a vague look on her face, like she wasn't sure the box she held was the right one.

"Ms. Shin," Aaron said, "that's the one for kids. The blue box. My sister takes it."

"Thank you, Aaron," she said, relieved, and took the blue box next to his. "My grandson's staying with me and he's burning up too."

Aaron watched the shelf empty out, box by box, at twelve dollars each. He turned it over in his head. Strawberries were cheap because there were mountains of them, and people still walked past. Medicine was double the price and everybody grabbed one anyway.

"So the strawberry price drops and people still only buy so many," he said slowly, "but the medicine price goes up and up and people keep buying it exactly the same."

Theo recounted what his father, who read economics books at breakfast, had told him last winter when the same thing happened. "My dad calls that inelastic," Theo said. "Demand for stuff people need, like medicine, changes little when the price changes."

"Then the store could charge anything," Aaron said, half a question.

His mother put the last box in the basket before he could wonder any further. "Come on," she said, "and grab some of those strawberries on the way out. At that price, we can afford two."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A result that shows the hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result and is worth reporting.
story:
Charles spread his bean seeds across the kitchen table like a general arranging tiny soldiers. His science fair project, he had decided, would prove that seeds sprouted faster in the warm cupboard above the stove than in the cold refrigerator. He wrote his hypothesis on an index card in his best handwriting, which was still fairly terrible, and taped it to a jar of damp paper towels. "Day one," he announced to the toaster. "Warm jar, fridge jar. May the best jar win."

By Thursday, the fridge jar had three fat white sprouts and the cupboard jar had exactly zero. Charles stared at them, then at his index card, then at the sprouts again, as if they might apologize and shrink back into their seeds. They did not. He checked the cupboard for clues. Warm, dark, damp. Nothing obviously wrong. He checked again at breakfast, at lunch, and once at nine at night in his pajamas, holding a flashlight like a detective. Still zero.

At school, Kallie took one look at his face and guessed everything. "Your beans turned out wrong, didn't they." Her own project sat proudly beside her lunchbox: a slice of bread in a plastic container, growing a fuzzy gray-green colony she had named Gerald. "Look at Gerald. He's shaped exactly like an intestine. He's going to make the whole gymnasium gag, and the judges are going to love it." That was Kallie's plan, plainly stated: first place, through maximum disgust.

Charles slid his data sheet across the table. "I can't present this. My hypothesis said warm, and warm lost. Three to zero." He was on the edge of throwing the whole project in the recycling bin, sprouts and all, when a rumor began to circulate through the cafeteria that Ms. Aquino had already picked out her favorite project, and that rumor was, everyone agreed, definitely about a potato battery and definitely unfair. Charles marched to Room 12 to complain about the potato, and found Ms. Aquino watering a fern instead.

"Nobody picked anything," she said. "There is no potato. But tell me about your beans." He showed her the data sheet, braced for her to say too bad, so sad. Instead she read it twice, nodded, and said, "This is good. A result that shows your hypothesis was wrong is still a real scientific result, and it is worth reporting. Present it exactly as it happened." Charles walked back to the cafeteria feeling like the fridge jar had won twice.

On fair day, he stood beside his poster, which said in enormous letters: I PREDICTED WRONG, AND HERE IS WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED. A judge read it, asked him three questions, and wrote things down. Later, when the ribbons were handed out, the class vote for favorite project was unanimous. Charles looked over at Kallie, who was holding a red second-place ribbon and glaring at Gerald the intestine like it had personally betrayed her. "Second," she muttered. "To beans. Cold beans." Charles patted his jar and said, "Gerald's still shaped like an intestine, though. That's gotta count for something."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Mia held the mixing bowl over the counter like a trophy, because tonight she was making banana muffins for the whole family, all by herself. Her dad would draft her little brother into setting the table, her mom had promised to stay out of the kitchen entirely, and Mia had the recipe spread out where she could see every step. She mashed the bananas until they smelled sweet and faintly nutty, cracked the eggs, and then opened the cabinet for the baking powder.

The tin rattled. Two teaspoons of powder, and she needed two full ones. Not nearly enough.

She texted Ajay first, because Ajay baked cookies every weekend and acted like a science tutor about it. "Out of baking powder," she typed. "Can I just use baking soda? Same thing, right?"

His answer came fast. "Not the same. Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid."

Mia stared at the message. A dry acid? She looked at the orange box of soda in her hand, then back at the recipe. Buttermilk, the recipe said, and buttermilk was nowhere in the fridge. Then she saw the last line of the ingredient list: plain yogurt. Sour stuff. She scooped a little onto her finger and tasted it, tangy and sharp, and a plan snapped together in her head so fast she laughed out loud.

Jayden wandered in to steal a banana and found Mia scribbling on the back of the recipe. "What are you doing?"

"Being skeptical of my own idea, then fixing it," she said. "I'm using baking soda instead of powder, but I'm doubling the yogurt so there's enough acid in the batter to react with it." She stirred the wet ingredients hard, watching the yogurt swirl in like a cloudy river, then folded the batter gently because the recipe underlined that word twice.

The muffins rose into golden domes, cracked a little on top, and filled the kitchen with a smell so warm that Jayden abandoned his banana on the spot. Her dad walked in, took one bite, and closed his eyes.

"Two more," he said, already reaching. "For science."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: Councils often send a proposed bylaw change to a committee first, which studies it and recommends whether the full council should approve it.
story:
Nevaeh spread the petition across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighting the corners with jars of pickled beets so the pages would not curl. Forty-seven people had signed it, asking the city to change the bylaw that banned skateboards on the library plaza, and today the city would say what happened next.

"That's a lot of names," said Phoenix, who had arrived with his helmet still on.

"Forty-seven," Nevaeh said. "Now what? Does the whole council just vote on it?" She had assumed that a petition went straight to a vote, the way a coin goes straight into a vending machine, but when she called the city clerk's office that morning, the woman on the phone had said the petition had been sent to the community services committee first.

"Committee," Phoenix repeated. "Like a smaller group that studies it?"

Jethro, who was reading over Nevaeh's shoulder, tapped the clerk's phone number. "So they look at it and recommend whether the full council should approve it. That's what the lady said. You wrote it down."

Nevaeh studied her notes. So the petition was like a river that hit a gate before it reached the sea. If the committee said no, the whole council might never even see it. Which meant forty-seven signatures might not be enough on their own. "We have to speak there too," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "At the committee. Not just the council meeting."

Her grandmother set down a plate of oatmeal cookies. "Your grandfather got the noise bylaw softened that way, back when this street was part of the old Campbell dynasty, before the wards changed."

"You mean a real dynasty?" Phoenix asked.

"A family that ran everything, close enough," her grandmother said. "Get yourselves over there. Wear something durable, those chairs at city hall are older than me."

The three of them packed the petition into Nevaeh's backpack, along with the cookies, and pedaled hard toward the yellow-brick building on Main Street, Phoenix ringing his bell the whole way.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl's official name was the AFL-NFL World Championship Game; the Roman numeral 'Super Bowl I' was added later.
story:
The community sports field had been turned into a viewing party for the championship game, with a giant screen propped against the backstop and half the neighbourhood spread across blankets on the grass. Ellie sat between her dad and Tobias, who had his trivia notebook balanced on one knee. Tobias wanted more than anything to win the library's sports trivia contest next weekend, and he was collecting facts like bottle caps.

"Why does the game use Roman numerals?" April asked, pointing at the huge painted banner near the concession stand. The banner depicted a golden trophy, a helmet, and the letters "LVIII" in tall red print.

"Because it's fancy," Tobias said. "That's the whole reason."

Ellie wasn't so sure. Fancy didn't explain anything. She thought about the numbers on the banner, and then about something her grandfather had once mentioned while flipping channels. She decided to test it. "If the Roman numerals were part of the name from the beginning, then the first one would have been called Super Bowl I right away, with the numeral in the name. But Grandpa said the first one had a different official name." She pulled out her phone and typed carefully, shielding the screen from the sun with her hand.

The answer came up, and she read it twice to be certain. "It was called the AFL-NFL World Championship Game. The Roman numerals were added later, after people started calling it Super Bowl I."

"So the numerals are like a nickname that stuck," April said slowly, watching the banner again.

"Better than a nickname," Tobias said, scribbling fast. "It's a contest question waiting to happen." He underlined it twice. "Nobody at the library is going to know that."

"You think everyone else is gullible," Ellie said, "just because they don't read your notebook."

"I think they're lucky I do," Tobias said.

On the field beside the screen, the tenant who rented the little equipment shed, a quiet man who refereed youth soccer on Saturdays, leaned over the fence and tipped his cap toward them. "First one I ever watched, we called it the championship game too," he said. "Never thought a number would end up bigger than the game."

The screen flared bright, the crowd on the blankets stirred, and the kickoff sailed up into the darkening sky.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Brooklyn spread her poster board across the library table and set her stack of surveys beside it. On the surveys, students had reported whether they ate breakfast and what their last math scores were. She had found that the breakfast eaters mostly had better scores, and she had typed "BREAKFAST MAKES YOU SMARTER" in giant letters.

Yasmine slid into the chair across from her and squinted at the title. "So if I eat a waffle tomorrow, my quiz goes up?"

"Basically," Brooklyn said.

Safa leaned over, chewing a granola bar. "My brother eats breakfast every day. He also failed a spelling test on Tuesday because he stayed up until two playing games."

Brooklyn looked at her data table. Half the breakfast eaters were the kids on the swim team, the ones who got up early anyway. She remembered her own surveys from last fall, when she had tried to prove that owning a dog made people more responsible, and Mr. Nowak had written one word in the margin: "Correlation?" She had ignored it, mostly because she did not know what it meant.

She flipped through the surveys again, this time sorting by bedtime. The breakfast eaters also mostly went to bed earlier. Kids who stayed up late skipped breakfast and did worse on tests, both because they were lethargic all morning and scrambling for the bus.

"Oh no," Brooklyn said. "The breakfast might not be causing anything. Something else, like bedtime, could be causing both."

"What do you call it when two things happen together like that?" Yasmine asked.

"Correlation," Brooklyn said, deleting her giant letters. "And it doesn't prove one thing causes the other."

She rebuilt the poster as a question instead of an answer, cutting a strip of cardboard to convert the blank board into a flip chart. Yasmine drew a waffle with a graduation cap on it for the cover, and Safa titled it "The Mysterious Third Factor" in her best artisan lettering, which looked suspiciously like fancy cereal-box writing.

By closing time, the poster asked "Does Breakfast Cause Good Grades, or Does Bedtime Cause Both?" and beneath it, in small letters, "Further testing required. Snacks welcome."

Yasmine held up the last granola bar. "For science," she said, and split it three ways.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
Charlotte had walked past Yousif's house every school day since second grade, but on Tuesday she crossed to the other side of the street, because Yousif had gone to the arcade on Saturday with Braxton and never even texted her. She had found out from a photo, three blurry figures leaning over a pinball machine, and the resentment had been sitting in her chest ever since, heavy as a backpack full of wet towels.

On Thursday she decided she could not cross the street forever. She wanted her best friend back, but she also did not want to shout, because shouting with Yousif usually ended in a week of silence. There had to be a better way to say it. That was the problem she chewed on all through Ms. Kaminski's class, half filling her notebook with attempts.

"You ditched me," she wrote, and crossed it out, because that sounded like an accusation, and Yousif would get defensive and stop listening. She tried again. "When I saw the photo, I felt left out." She stared at that one. It said the same thing but pointed at her own feelings instead of at him. It felt softer, like a door left unlocked instead of slammed.

The next morning she caught Yousif on his porch, tying one sneaker. "Hey," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she planned. "When I saw that arcade photo, I felt left out. Like everybody forgot me."

Yousif looked up. "Braxton asked me Saturday morning and I said yes before I even thought. I figured you were at your grandma's." He paused. "I should have texted anyway. I'm sorry."

"It's called an I-message," Charlotte said. "Braxton told me about it. He said a psychologist named Thomas Gordon came up with it in the 1960s. You say 'I felt' instead of 'you did,' so nobody feels attacked."

"You got that from Braxton?"

"He got it from his sister. Whatever. It worked." A cat slunk along the fence, low and predatory, eyes fixed on something in the grass, and then pounced on a leaf and sat there looking disappointed. They both laughed, and the laugh felt like the first warm day after winter.

"So, arcade this weekend?" Yousif asked. "All three of us, and I'll send the text myself."

"Deal," said Charlotte. "And I'll actually answer it."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Scrabble players often settle arguments about whether a word is allowed by agreeing, before the game, on one dictionary to check.
story:
Evelyn had never noticed how many weird little objects lived in Grandma's hallway drawer until the rainy afternoon when the power went out. There were thimbles, a magnifying glass, and a box of Scrabble tiles that smelled like pencil shavings. She carried it to the kitchen table, where her friend Chelsea was visiting and Caden, the boy from next door, had already claimed the window seat.

They were twenty minutes into the game when Chelsea laid down Q and I and announced, "Qi. Twenty-one points, because the Q is on a double letter."

"That is not a word," Caden said. "You can't just put two letters down and call it a thing."

"It is too a word. It's like, energy."

"Then prove it." Caden crossed his arms, and Evelyn could see the whole afternoon curling up and dying right there, like a leaf in Grandma's woodstove. Nobody had a phone that worked without the router. Grandma offered three dictionaries from the shelf, which was the problem: one was so old it called a refrigerator an "icebox," and another was a pocket version that seemed to skip everything after "plume." Chelsea said the old one counted because old dictionaries knew more words. Caden said the pocket one counted because it was newer. Evelyn drummed her fingers on the table and wondered how something as small as a two-letter word could cause such a giant argument.

"Wait," she said. "Maybe the problem isn't the word. Maybe the problem is that we never picked which dictionary is the boss." She proposed a quick negotiation: before any word got challenged, they would delegate the deciding to one single book, chosen now, while everyone was still calm. They picked the big red one from the den. Caden flipped to the Q section, muttering the alphabet under his breath like a spell.

"Qi," he read, his voice going sour. "A vital life force in Chinese thought." He squinted at Chelsea. "Fine. Twenty-one points. But if I put down 'zyn' next turn, the red book decides, and you can't argue."

"Deal," Evelyn said, and slid the dictionary to the middle of the table where everyone could reach it.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
story:
At Gate 14, Jeremy watched the departure board flip from DELAYED to BOARDING, and his stomach did a small flip of its own. His family was flying to Portugal, six hours ahead of home time, and his dad had already promised they would walk along the river their first evening there. Jeremy had a plan for those first evenings, or at least the beginning of one. His friend Riaan had sent him off that morning with a warning: "My cousin flew to Europe last summer and said they were zombies for a week. Nobody could sleep at night." Jeremy wanted to test whether that was really true, or just one family being dramatic.

He started a page in his notebook before the plane even pushed back. At the top he wrote: midnight at home versus midnight in Lisbon. Then he made two columns, one for what the clock on the wall said and one for how awake he felt. His little sister slept through dinner and the movie, which fit Riaan's story. Jeremy stayed awake too, but that proved nothing, because he was excited.

The real test came on the second night. In the apartment his parents had rented, the street below was dark and the refrigerator hummed in the corner, and the clock said 12:40. Jeremy was wide awake, and so were his dad and his sister, whispering over a card game in the kitchen. Only his mom had gone to bed, and he could hear her turning over. On the third night it was the same: 1:15, cards shuffling, everyone's eyes bright as noon. Jeremy wrote it down.

By the fourth night, something had shifted. His sister fell asleep at eleven, local time, without a fight. On the fifth night his dad yawned at ten and gave up on the crossword. Jeremy looked at his columns and counted the nights. Six hours of time difference. One night closer to normal for every hour. He sat on the bathroom floor so the light wouldn't wake anyone and did the math again. One day for each hour, exactly, the way water drains out of a tub at a steady rate.

The next morning he found a postcard stand near the bakery and bought one for Riaan. He wrote the rule in two sentences, then added, "I tested it myself. It took our whole family six nights." Ms. Bélanger, his former teacher who lived on Riaan's street, had once told their class that a good scientist could enroll anyone in an experiment just by making it interesting. Jeremy decided his evidence was unanimous: four out of four family members, all adjusting at the same steady pace.

On the seventh night, the whole apartment was asleep before ten except Jeremy, who lay listening to the quiet street. He got up, padded to the window, and looked down at the river his dad had promised, black and gleaming under the lamps. Tomorrow they would walk along it in daylight, and he would be awake enough to actually see it. He pressed his forehead to the cool glass and whispered, "Worth every sleepy night."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal.
story:
The storm was supposed to hit by evening, and Mya's mother had sent her to the gas station on the corner with a list: batteries, granola bars, and two bottles of water. The parking lot was full. Inside, people were carrying baskets piled with canned soup and flashlight batteries, and a man by the coolers was taking the last four cases of water off the shelf.

Mya got in line behind Tyler, who was holding a single bottle of water and a bag of chips. "Three dollars for this," Tyler said, turning the bottle so she could see the sticker slapped over the old price. "It was a dollar twenty-five this morning. I was here this morning. My mom sent me back for a second one."

"That's twice as much," Mya said. "That's more than twice as much." She looked at the shelf behind them, where one lone bottle of sparkling water sat alone between empty rows. Then she thought of the gas station out by the highway, the big one with thirty pumps, where nobody from their street ever shopped because it was too far to walk. "Come on," she said, and pulled Tyler toward the door.

At the big station, the water aisle was full. Cases stacked to the ceiling, coolers humming, and a hand-written sign that said WATER $1.25. Mya picked up two bottles. "Same water," she said. "Same brand, same size. It's a dollar twenty-five here because there's a wall of it, and three dollars at the corner because there were four cases left." Tyler paid for his second bottle and tore the corner store's sticker off the first one, holding them side by side like evidence.

"It's like Mr. Sato's homework," Tyler said as they walked back. "We had to read a page from this guy, Adam Smith. In 'The Wealth of Nations', published in 1776, he says nothing is more useful than water, yet water will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." He squinted. "I didn't get it until right now, standing in that empty aisle."

"You need water to live," Mya said. "You don't need a diamond for anything. But water's everywhere, so it's cheap." At the corner station, the man from the coolers was now taping a new sign to the register: WATER SOLD OUT. The cashier was restishing nothing behind the counter, just counting the drawer, and Mya guessed the store's revenue today would be its best of the whole month.

Back home, her mother looked at the receipt. "You incorporated a whole economics lesson into one errand," she said, handing Mya a granola bar from the bag. Mya shrugged. "Tyler says next storm, we buy diamonds instead." From the driveway, Tyler yelled, "No, next storm, we buy the water early and incorporate a markup."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure deep underground without fully melting.
story:
The old quarry above town had become Mr. Goldberg's outdoor classroom, and today he had dumped three buckets of rocks on a folding table. "Sort them," he said. "Igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic. You have until noon." Matteo picked up a dark rock with thin wavy stripes, like frosting swirled through a cake. "That one got cooked," he said, dropping it onto the igneous pile. "Igneous means melted, so anything hot goes there." Lilou frowned but didn't argue, because arguing with Matteo before lunch was never worth it.

Eva worked slowly, holding each rock up so the sun refracted through a quartz vein and threw a small rainbow on her notebook. She pulled a striped rock from the igneous pile and turned it over. "If this melted, the stripes would be gone. Melted stuff mixes." Matteo snatched it back. "Then it wasn't hot enough to melt all the way." Eva raised an eyebrow. "So it was hot, and squeezed, and it didn't melt. It changed. What's a rock called when it changes?"

Mr. Goldberg, who was sitting on a stable stack of slate nearby pretending to read, lowered his book. "Metamorphic," he said, and turned a page. That was all. Matteo stared at the striped rock in his hand. He licked his thumb and rubbed the surface, testing the idea that a changed rock would look somehow newer, softer. It didn't. It looked like the limestone down the hill, but pressed, folded, cooked without ever becoming liquid. He thought of bread dough squeezed through fingers, reshaped but never poured.

He rebuilt the piles. The swirly striped ones moved to a new middle pile, and he found more: a rock with glittery layers that had once been plain mudstone, a hard gray one folded like a wrinkled shirt. "Okay," he said to Eva. "I was wrong. Heated doesn't mean melted. Metamorphic means changed by heat and squeezing, deep down, and it never has to melt at all." Eva added her rainbow-making quartz to his pile. "The rock collectors' guild accepts your apology," she said, and held up the next specimen to the light.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
story:
Juliette laid out her supplies on the kitchen table: a jar of water, three paint tubes, a canvas board, and the best brushes from Mr. Otieno's art room. He had let her borrow them for the weekend because she was painting a portrait of her grandmother's old residence, the blue house with the crooked porch where Grandma had lived for forty years.

Greta arrived first, then Joel, and they both leaned over the sketch Juliette had taped to the table. "You drew the porch railing better than I could," Greta said. Joel was already squeezing paint onto a palette, blobs of cobalt and white and a dot of gold for the porch light.

The painting went well for an hour. Juliette mixed the blues thin and runny, adding water from the jar whenever the paint got too thick, and the sky spread across the canvas in smooth strokes. Then Joel stood up to get snacks and left his brush lying on the table, its bristles loaded with paint, while he searched the cupboard for crackers. He took his time. When he came back and picked up the brush, he frowned. The bristles had gone stiff, and they held their shape like little frozen fingers.

"That's ruined," he said, pulling at them. Water did nothing. He dunked the brush in the jar and scrubbed it against the bottom, but the bristles stayed hard.

Juliette looked at her own brush, still wet and soft, then at Joel's. Hers had been sitting in the water jar between strokes, and Joel's had been sitting in open air. She thought about the sky she had just painted, how it was already dry to the touch, and how the paint in the tube stayed soft because the tube was sealed tight. "It's the drying," she said slowly. "While the paint is wet, water thins it out, that's why the jar works. But once it dries, it turns water-resistant. That's why your brush won't clean now, and why my sky doesn't smear when I touch it."

"So we have to wash the brushes before the paint dries on them," Greta said, and she fetched a second jar of clean water for rinsing between every color change.

They worked out a system to conserve their remaining good brushes. Juliette set a paper towel by each jar so a wet brush never touched the table, and Joel kept time out loud, calling "rinse" whenever somebody paused too long. At the end, they washed every brush with soap and laid them flat to dry.

When Mr. Otieno came by on Monday to see the finished painting, he stood in front of the blue house for a long moment. "That porch light," he said. "It's eloquent. You can almost hear the crickets." Juliette grinned and handed him the brush case, every one soft and clean, and Joel held up the one ruined brush like a trophy of what they had learned.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Most vegetable seeds need water, oxygen and warmth to germinate, but not light; a few, such as lettuce, sprout better with light and are sown very shallowly.
story:
Piper knelt on her apartment balcony with a bag of potting soil, six containers, and a paper envelope of lettuce seeds she had bought with her allowance. Down in the courtyard, the community garden beds sat empty of lettuce, though Caylee had planted a whole row there three weeks ago. Not one sprout had come up. "Maybe the seeds were bad," Caylee had said, but Piper wanted to evaluate that idea herself before she believed it.

She filled her containers and pressed the tiny seeds deep into the soil, a full finger's length down, the way the tomato and bean packets had shown. Tomatoes and beans were already up in her warm corner by the door, where she watered them every morning. She kept the lettuce containers beside them, warm and damp, and waited.

Ten days passed. Nothing. Piper tapped the soil, checked that it was moist, and felt the warmth of the balcony bricks. Water, warmth, air; the soil was loose, so the seeds had oxygen too. "It's like a jury that can't agree," she told Margaux, who had come up to see the tomatoes. "Everything looks right, but the verdict is no sprouts." Margaux leaned over the pots and frowned.

Then Piper read her lettuce packet again, the part she had skipped. Sow shallowly, it said, barely cover the seeds, because lettuce sprouts best with light. She sat back on her heels. The courtyard seeds had been buried deep too. That was it. Seeds like tomatoes and beans needed water, oxygen and warmth, and light didn't matter to them, but lettuce was different.

She sowed a new tray, pressing the seeds into the surface and dusting them with the thinnest sprinkle of soil. "That hardly counts as planting," Margaux said. "It counts as not being reckless with depth," Piper said, and set the tray where the morning sun touched it.

Four days later, a haze of green freckled the soil, tiny and even, like pepper shaken across a plate. Piper ran to the railing and called down to the courtyard, where Caylee was kneeling by the empty row with a fresh packet in her hand. "Don't bury them this time," Piper called. "Just tickle them into the top of the soil and leave them in the light."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A control group gets no change at all, giving a baseline to compare the tested groups against.
story:
Everly lined up nine bean plants along the back counter of the science classroom, each one in a paper cup labeled with a letter. Cups A, B, and C would get the fancy fertilizer from the garden store. Cups D, E, and F would get half strength. And cup G would get plain water and nothing else. "It's my control group," she told Dan, who was building a volcano two tables away. "It gets no change at all, so I can compare everything against it."

"Seems boring," Dan said. He wanted the blue ribbon so badly he had painted his volcano three times, and he kept glancing at Everly's cups like they were competition. "Nobody wins with beans."

Two weeks later, Everly measured the plants and her stomach dropped. The fertilizer plants were fine, but the control plant, cup G, was the tallest of all. That made no sense. Plain water shouldn't do that, and if her control was wrong, her whole poster was wrong. She checked the leaves, made a careful diagnosis, early rot, maybe overwatering, but the plant looked healthy. Something hidden was going on.

Then she noticed the dirt in cup G was dark and rich, darker than the dirt in her other cups. On Friday she hid behind Mr. Gallagher's supply cabinet at lunch and waited, hardly breathing, her knees cramping on the cold tile floor. The door creaked. Anas slipped in with a small green bottle and tipped it into cup G.

"Anas!"

He froze. "My grandmother says fertilizer helps everything. I wanted your control to win. I didn't know which cup was which." He pointed at the cup. "Anonymous plant hero, that was the plan."

Everly laughed, then stopped. "You contaminated my baseline. I have to start over with a new control." She dumped cup G into the bin and planted a fresh seed, and Dan, watching from the doorway, set down his paintbrush.

"Guess controls aren't boring after all," he said. "Want help labeling the new cups?"

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Adding the tops and the bottoms separately gives a wrong answer: one half plus one third is five sixths, not two fifths.
story:
Madison spread her homework across the library table by the window, where the afternoon light made the pencil marks easy to see. Her ambition for the week was simple: finish every fraction problem before Friday, so she could join the weekend baking day her neighbour was hosting. The only trouble was the page in front of her, which asked her to add one half and one third.

Across the table, Augustin was chewing his pencil. He wrote something, crossed it out, and wrote it again. Skylar sat between them, stacking her books into a tidy tower, because Skylar liked the library shelves to look orderly even when her own notebook was a mess.

"I got two fifths," Augustin said at last, turning his paper around. "One plus one is two, and two plus three is five. So two fifths."

Skylar leaned over and looked at his answer. "Try this," she said. "You started with one half. Is your answer bigger than a half?"

Augustin drew a line on his scrap paper and marked it into five equal pieces. He shaded two of them, then stared at it. His answer, two fifths, was smaller than the half he had started with. "That can't be right," he said slowly. "When I add something, I should end up with more, not less."

Madison pulled her paper closer and tried the same trick with her own problem. She drew a half, then a third, then tried to see how they might fit together. The pieces were different sizes, like puzzle pieces from two different boxes. She thought she could diagnose the exact trouble: the bottom numbers did not match, so the pieces could not be counted straight across. She flipped to the back of her textbook, past the section on equivalent fractions, hunting for the page Ms. Otieno had mentioned on Monday.

"Sixths," she said suddenly. "Both of them can turn into sixths."

She wrote it out. One half became three sixths. One third became two sixths. Now the pieces matched, and she counted them like ordinary things: three pieces plus two pieces made five pieces. Five sixths. She checked it against her drawing, and the shaded bar stretched past the halfway mark, exactly as an answer should.

Ms. Otieno passed by their table on her way to the returns cart and paused long enough to see Madison's paper. "Testing it with a picture first," she said. "That's a good habit." She moved on without saying anything more, which suited Madison fine.

Madison slid her notebook toward Augustin so he could see how the sixths lined up, top and bottom. His pencil hovered over his own page, and his usually rebellious habit of arguing back seemed to have gone quiet. He copied the method once, twice, then covered his work with his hand and tried a new problem alone.

"Eight fifteenths," he announced a minute later. "Want to check me?"

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: Stating the problem as a shared question, like "We disagree about whether the ball was out," keeps the talk on the rule instead of on who is to blame.
story:
The argument at the tetherball pole had been going for two minutes, and Grayson could hear it from the canoe rack. Aubrie stood with her hands on her hips while Thea pointed at a scuffed line in the dirt. "The ball was out. You saw it," Aubrie said. "I did not cheat," Thea shot back, and Grayson noticed that every time somebody said the word cheat, the argument got more volatile, like a fire fed with dry leaves. His ankle tendon, sore from yesterday's hike, twinged as he jogged over, and he tried to regulate his breathing the way the swim instructor had taught them, slow in, slow out, because it was hard to think when you were puffed up.

"Okay, wait," Grayson said. "Can I try something? Don't say who's wrong. Just say what we disagree about." Thea crossed her arms but nodded. Aubrie frowned. "We disagree about whether the ball was out," Grayson said, pointing at the line. He was surprised at how different the sentence felt from you're wrong. It was like the problem had climbed off of Aubrie and landed on the ground between them, where everybody could look at it.

That night he wrote a letter to his older brother, who was at a different camp across the lake.

Dear Marcus, I found a weird trick today. When Aubrie and Thea fought about the call, I made them name the problem as one question both of them owned, and then they stopped yelling at each other and started arguing about the line itself. They still fought, but about dirt, which was funnier. Thea got down on her knees with a magnifying lens from nature crafts. Tomorrow we vote on a rule that both teams agree to before the game starts. Wish me luck. Your brother, Grayson.

The next morning, Thea taped a sign to the pole: FAIR RULE, DECIDED BY EVERYONE. Aubrie read it twice, then pulled out a marker and added, AND THE LINE GETS REPAINTED EVERY MONDAY. She had changed her mind about the whole thing, Grayson realized, somewhere between the magnifying lens and the marker. At lunch, three kids from Cabin Four came over to ask how the rule worked, and Grayson pushed his tray aside, ready to explain.

"First," he said, "tell me what you disagree about."

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
The waiting room smelled like hand sanitizer and old magazines, and Ivy sat twisting the hem of her jacket so hard it was starting to look like a raisin. She was there for her flu shot, which last week had seemed like no big deal. Then Charly had told her about a cousin whose arm swelled up "like a balloon animal" after one, and how he couldn't lift it for a whole month, and now every time Ivy closed her eyes she saw that balloon arm floating over her like a parade float. She hadn't even told her dad why she'd gone quiet in the car. He'd just said, "Big day, huh," and handed her a peppermint.

The waiting room itself was barren, almost empty, just a fern losing a slow war with the fluorescent lights and two other patients: a man asleep with a crossword on his chest, and Ms. Paquette from two streets over, knitting something green. Ivy picked up a pamphlet from the rack just to have something to do with her hands. It was about why people fear rare things, and one paragraph stopped her cold. In 1973, it said, psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described what they called the availability heuristic, meaning that people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.

Ivy read it twice. She thought of Charly's cousin and his parade-float arm. The story came to mind instantly, bright and vivid, which the pamphlet seemed to imply meant her brain would act like swollen arms happened all the time. She decided to run a test, right there, because sitting still was worse. "Ms. Paquette," she said, "do you know anybody who had a really bad reaction to a flu shot?"

Ms. Paquette looked up over her needles. "Can't say I do, dear. I've had one every year since I was your age. Worst that happened was I felt tired and watched game shows all afternoon." Ivy asked the sleeping man too, who woke up, blinked, and said, "I got one Tuesday. It stung for four seconds. I timed it. I was proud of that." Then he went back to sleep. Two people, zero balloon arms. Charly's one story was loud, but it was one story.

"Availability heuristic," Ivy said to herself, quietly, tasting the words. Ms. Paquette smiled like she recognized them.

"Nurse said one thing to remember, though," Ms. Paquette added. "It works both ways. Easy to remember doesn't mean often true."

When the nurse called her name, Ivy stood up so fast the pamphlet slid to the floor, and she felt in her pocket to make sure the peppermint was still there. Her arm already stung in imagination, four seconds' worth, but she walked through the door anyway.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: According to the American Academy of Dermatology, about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne.
story:
Cameron stood at the sink in the boys' bathroom and studied his forehead in the mirror. Three red spots had appeared overnight, right above his left eyebrow, and they seemed to have plans to multiply. He was supposed to give his candidate speech for class representative in twenty minutes, in front of everyone, and the last thing he needed was a face that looked like a science experiment.

He turned on the tap and scrubbed his forehead with soap, hard, the way he thought you were supposed to. The spots got redder. He scrubbed again. Worse still. That was strange, he thought. If dirt was causing them, washing should help. But it hadn't, which meant the cause was something he couldn't see, something under the skin, and scrubbing was just making things angrier. The idea germinated slowly in his head: maybe the problem wasn't on the surface at all.

The door banged open and Jean came in, dragging Manuel by the sleeve. "I told you he'd be hiding in here," Jean said. "Mr. Aziz has been looking everywhere. You're up after Ravi."

"I can't," Cameron said. "Look at my face."

Manuel leaned against the sink and looked, really looked, not laughing. "My sister had that exact same thing last year," he said. "She was so upset my mom took her to the dermatologist."

"What's a dermatologist?" Cameron asked.

"Skin doctor. She came home and told me something weird. She said about 85 percent of people between ages 12 and 24 get at least minor acne. That's basically everybody."

"Eighty-five percent," Cameron repeated. He did the math against his class of twenty-six. That was around twenty-two kids. Twenty-two faces with the same red spots hiding under the same careful haircuts, including probably the two boys standing right here. "So Ravi has it too?"

Jean snorted. "Ravi has it so bad he grows sideburns to cover it. Come on, it's not a disease, it's just being twelve."

Cameron looked at the mirror one more time. His hair was still pushed forward like a curtain, the way he'd fixed it that morning, which explained why his forehead had been an oily, sweaty mess all week. He'd stopped showering at night too, ever since basketball practice moved to mornings, and he'd skipped the deodorant his mom bought because the label said it was for men and he wasn't one yet. But maybe that was backwards. Maybe this was exactly the age when all of it started to matter, the shower, the deodorant, the whole routine, invisible things you did for invisible causes.

He splashed cold water on his forehead, gently this time, and pushed his hair up off his face. He dug the deodorant stick out of his backpack, where it had been germinating at the bottom for two weeks, and used it.

"When I get up there," he said, "I'm telling them my first act as class rep is putting a box of face wash in the gym bathroom."

Jean held the door. "That's actually not the worst campaign promise I've ever heard."

Cameron walked out with his whole face showing.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many school pools are 25 yards or 25 meters long, called short course, while Olympic swimming races are held in 50-meter pools, called long course.
story:
The locker room smelled like chlorine and rubber flip-flops, and Willow sat on the bench with her tryout card trembling in her damp hands. Ms. Sandhu had pinned the team list to the corkboard by the pool door: anyone who wanted the last spot on the swim team had to beat the cutoff time in tomorrow's trial heat. Willow's card said her best time from summer club was 41 seconds for 50 freestyle, but the cutoff was 38, and the trial heat was in ten minutes.

"That's a contradiction," said Kaysen, peering over her shoulder while stuffing his sneakers into his locker. "You beat kids all summer. How can you be three whole seconds too slow now?" He wasn't on the team himself, but he came to every tryout to yell for her from the bleachers.

Willow chewed the strap of her goggles. Something felt wrong, and it wasn't just nerves. Her summer club practiced in a huge pool, the one downtown with the diving well, while the school pool was so short she counted only a few strokes before hitting the wall. She tried to conserve her energy on the walk to the pool deck, breathing slowly, because Coach only allowed each swimmer one warm-up lap before time trials began.

Ziad was stretching by the lane ropes, and he saw her staring down the length of the pool. "What are you looking at?"

"I swam my summer times in a 50-meter pool," Willow said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "Olympic races are held in 50-meter pools. That's called long course." She pointed at the wall she'd have to turn at, way too soon. "School pools like this one are usually 25 yards or 25 meters. That's called short course. So my 41 seconds from the big pool can't be compared with what I'll swim here. It's a different race, even if it sounds the same."

"Then your card time is biased," Ziad said. "It makes you look slower than you are."

Or faster, Willow thought grimly, and there was only one way to find out. The whistle blew. She pulled her cap down, stepped onto the block, and gripped the edge with her toes. Ms. Sandhu raised her clipboard.

"Swimmers, take your marks."

Willow crouched low, staring at the far wall, and when the beep cracked through the humid air she dove.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: The flutter kick in front crawl should come from the hips with fairly straight legs, since kicking mostly from the knees creates drag.
story:
The community centre had the rink on one side of the hallway and the pool on the other, so Addison could hear skates scraping while she stood shivering at the shallow end in her swimsuit. Through the big window, her friend Raylan was orbiting the ice in slow loops, waiting for Sullivan to finish his goalie drills so they could play one-on-one until Addison's lesson ended. Raylan wanted to score on Sullivan more than anything, and he'd told her that morning, "He's never let me get one past him. Not once."

Mr. Aziz, the lifeguard, blew his whistle. "Twenty-five metres, front crawl, whenever you're ready, Addison." Addison pushed off and kicked like a frog in a blender. Her legs pumped and churned, her knees bending hard on every beat, and she grabbed the wall having travelled maybe five metres, breathing like a dragon. A boy in the next lane, all knobby knees and easy arms, slid past her barely making a splash. That was the part that bothered her.
