He wasn't trying even half as hard, and he was crossing the pool like a torpedo while she puttered like a bathtub toy.

She floated on her back and thought. Her kick came from her knees, bent and frantic, but his legs stayed almost straight, like two long oars, and the movement seemed to start higher up, at his hips. Maybe her knees were the problem. Maybe all that bending was dragging on the water like a parachute. She had to test it. She pushed off again, kept her legs fairly straight, and let the kick come from her hips instead. It felt lazy at first, like she was barely doing anything, but the tiles of the pool floor slid past faster than before. She turned her head to the side, took a breath, turned back, and kept going. The far wall arrived under her hand.

"That's the one!" Mr. Aziz called, and the boy in the next lane gave her a thumbs up between strokes.

Raylan appeared at the window, hair dripping sweat, holding his stick like a trophy. "I scored on Sullivan! Five-hole! Did you see my lap?" He pointed at the ice, where Sullivan stood in the goalie net, shaking his mitt at the ceiling.

"I was busy," Addison said, grinning, "but watch this." She set off again, hips driving her kick, straight legs slicing, one side breath, two, three, and her hand slapped the wall. She looked up at the window and Raylan shouted, muffled through the glass, "Now who's the five-hole?"

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Typing a message in all capital letters is widely read as shouting in online communication.
story:
The group chat had been quiet all afternoon, which was strange, because Elora usually posted at least eleven messages before lunch. Emile refreshed the chat on his tablet and stared at the last message, which was from Nellie: "Meet at the park at 4?" Nobody had answered. He wondered whether the others were busy, or whether the message had just slipped up the screen and gotten lost, the way a message could when nobody replied and it sank under newer things.

At 3:52, Elora's name lit up the chat. The message read, in huge letters, "WHERE ARE YOU." Emile sat back. The letters looked enormous on his screen, like Elora had smashed the keyboard with both fists. A second later, Nellie replied, "why are you yelling?" Emile read that twice. Yelling? Elora hadn't made a single sound.

He typed back, "we're coming, meet at the swings." Then, quietly, without the others seeing, he opened a private message to Elora and wrote, "why all caps?" A private chat was different, he had noticed. It was like whispering behind a cupped hand at lunch, while the group chat was more like standing up in the middle of the cafeteria and shouting something everyone could read.

Elora's reply came fast. "nobody answered nellie so i thought caps would get noticed." Emile tilted his head. So the capitals weren't anger at all. She had used them like a bright flag, something to make people look. It was a strange rule, he thought, that big letters made people hear shouting even when nobody was shouting. Where had that rule even come from? Could you find it written down anywhere, or did everyone just agree on it somehow?

At the park, Elora was kicking wood chips near the swings, her phone still in her hand. "Did it work?" she asked. "Did everyone see it?"

"Everybody saw it," Nellie said, arriving on her bike with one pedal still spinning. "Emile's little brother learned about engines this week and even he saw it. He keeps saying 'piston' at dinner."

"That's a machine part," Emile said. "And capitals are like that too. They push the message harder." Elora frowned, then grinned, and pulled out her phone. She typed something and held the screen up so they could both read it. It said, "sorry i yelled. sort of."

"It's fine," Nellie said. "Just do it again if the chat goes quiet for a whole hour."

"Deal," Elora said, and typed one more message into the group chat, small letters, all lowercase: "ok but next time you two answer faster." She pressed send, pocketed the phone, and ran for the swings.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homesickness is the distress of being away from home and familiar people; it is common after a move and usually eases as a person settles in.
story:
Emilia counted the boxes in the empty living room of apartment 4C. Thirteen boxes, one cat carrier, and zero friends. Back in her old town, she and Maggie had run a two-person detective guild that met every Saturday, and here there was nothing to detect, unless you counted the strange smell drifting from apartment 3A.

On the fourth morning, Emilia cried into a photo of her old street, the one with the crooked oak and Maggie waving from her porch. She hated that it kept happening. It made no sense, either, because the new apartment was fine, and the new school was fine, so something had to be causing it. She decided to investigate, the way the guild would. She took a notebook and wrote down every time the heavy feeling hit, then looked for a pattern. The notes said: Monday, seeing the photo. Tuesday, hearing her old ringtone. Wednesday, passing a girl in the hallway who laughed like Maggie.

"Hypothesis," she wrote. "It only shows up when something reminds me of home. So maybe if I add new things, the reminders will dwindle." It was a guess about something she could not see, some hidden rule working inside her, but a guess could be tested.

The test was simple. Each day she added one new thing: she learned the names of three neighbors, including Ms. Fitzgerald, who lived downstairs and fed pigeons from her window; she found the bodega that sold the same brand of hot chocolate as the shop on her old street; and she wrote down the smell from 3A, which turned out to be curry, and which Ms. Fitzgerald said came every Friday at six.

By the second Friday, Emilia still teared up at the photo, but only a little, and only for a minute. In the courtyard after school, a girl named Iyla asked what she was writing, then stole the notebook and read her hypothesis out loud in a dramatic announcer voice. "The detective guild needs a local chapter," Iyla declared, "and I already have a case. Somebody keeps leaving mitten yarn on the stairs, and the pattern is volatile, one day green, one day gray, no warning."

Emilia laughed, a real one, the first since the move. That night she video-called Maggie and told her about the yarn mystery, and about the crying, too, because a guild partner deserved the whole file. "My mom calls that homesickness," Maggie said. "It just means missing home and your people. It's basically the official moving side effect."

Emilia wrote it in the notebook: homesickness, being away from home and familiar people, common after a move, usually eases as you settle in. Then, underneath it, she wrote Saturday's plan, underlined twice. "Yarn stakeout, stairs, six o'clock. Bring snacks. Case 002."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
Quinn stood at the phone counter with her mother, watching the cashier run the final settlement for her very first phone. "Bus leaves in twenty minutes," her mother said, tapping the counter. Quinn slid the box open right there, because she wanted the flashlight app installed before the mall lights went dim in the parking garage.

She found the app and pressed install. Then a box popped up on the screen, and she winced. The flashlight app wanted permission to use her contacts. All of them. It also wanted her microphone and her camera. A flashlight needs light, she thought, not Avleen's phone number. Behind her, Stefan waved from the accessory shop across the aisle. "Quinn! Try the glow puzzle app, it's amazing!"

Stefan hurried over, his own phone in hand. "Watch, you tilt it and the pieces light up." He held out his screen, and Quinn noticed something odd. The top of his phone showed a tiny green dot, glowing steadily, even though he was only showing her a puzzle. She borrowed the demo phone on the counter and checked. On the puzzle app's page it listed the same strange permissions: camera, microphone, contacts.

"It's not logical," she said. "A puzzle doesn't need to hear me." She pressed install anyway on the demo, denied every permission it asked for, and the game still ran fine. Then she dug into the phone's settings and found the permissions listed there, with little switches beside them. "You can take permission away later in settings," she told Stefan, and she reached over and flicked off his puzzle app's microphone. The green dot vanished.

Stefan stared at the dark dot, then at her. "Wait. Mine's been on how long?"

Quinn grabbed the box, receipt and bag, and caught her mother's sleeve. Ten minutes to the bus. Stefan raced alongside them, already scrolling. "Quinn, it also had my camera on. Can you look at my settings too?"

"Meet me at school," she called over her shoulder, phone warm in her pocket. "First bell, seven forty-five."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Molten rock underground is called magma; once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.
story:
Cole crouched at the tide line with three plastic buckets labeled igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic, wondering which bucket deserved the speckled gray rock in his hand. Winnie dropped a black stone into the igneous bucket without hesitating.

"That one's easy," she said. "It came out of a volcano, so it's magma rock."

"Lava rock," said Shreya, from her perch on a driftwood log. "Not magma."

"It's the same thing, Shreya."

"It's not. Molten rock underground is called magma, but once it erupts onto the surface it's called lava." Shreya said it fast, like she'd been saving it.

Cole turned the speckled rock over. Yesterday Ms. Liu had set a chunk of glassy basalt on his desk and asked where it had cooled. He'd guessed wrong then, deep underground, and she'd only smiled and said to look for bubbles. Now he held the rock up to the light and saw tiny frothy holes, like a chocolate bar someone had whipped with a fork. Bubbles meant gas, and gas meant air, which meant the rock had melted out in the open. Not magma. Lava. Igneous, bucket one.

"Winnie," he said, "look at the holes. If it cooled down there, underground, no bubbles. This one erupted." He set it in the igneous bucket with a click.

Winnie frowned, picked up her black stone, squinted at it, then held it out. "Okay, fine, what about this one?"

Out past the breakers a fishing boat roared by, its propeller churning white water, and gulls wheeled up screaming as if a storm were imminent. Cole wished he could coordinate a drone to fly over the cliff at the beach's far end, where dark bands of rock slanted down toward the water, some layers tilted and wavy like someone had folded a sandwich. Metamorphic, probably. But for now he had Winnie's stone.

"Bubbles," he said, pointing at its surface, "and look, little sparkles. That's the same stuff as mine."

Winnie dropped it back in the igneous bucket and grabbed another rock. "Test me on the next one."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
The argument started over the potato salad, which was typical for Aunt Renata's backyard parties. Jacqueline, Ellie's cousin, had brought a beaded bracelet she made at her grandmother's reserve up north, and Sarina, who lived next door and had crashed the party because her own family reunion got rained out, took one look at it and said, "You don't count as Anishinaabe, though. Your mom's not status, right? My uncle says you have to prove it with a card."

"The card," Jacqueline said, "is not the boss of me."

Ellie chewed her forkful of potato salad and watched. She liked watching these two, because their opinions tended to fluctuate depending on who had spoken last, which meant the argument could pivot from bracelet to card to blood quantum to Sarina's uncle, sometimes all in one breath. But underneath all that swerving, she noticed a fixed question neither of them had said out loud: who actually gets to decide which group a person belongs to? The card people? The uncles? The person herself?

She had a theory. If belonging were only about cards, then nobody whose paperwork had burned in a fire, or gotten lost, or never been issued, could ever belong to anyone, and that seemed too dumb to be a real rule. Real rules usually got written down somewhere bigger than an uncle's opinion. So she pulled out her phone behind the dessert table and typed in "who decides if you are Indigenous international."

The answer came up fast. She read it twice, then walked back to the picnic table and held the phone out between them like a plate of something.

"United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples," she read. "Adopted on 13 September 2007. It says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

"That's it?" Sarina said. "Peoples, plural. Meaning the nations."

"Meaning not your uncle," Jacqueline said.

Sarina frowned at the screen, clearly checking whether she'd been gullible, then shrugged. "Fine. Then I'm telling him at Thanksgiving. Also, your bracelet is better than the ones he makes, but don't tell him I said that."

"Too late," said Jacqueline, threading the bracelet onto Sarina's wrist. "It's yours now, that's the rule."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Alice crouched beside the camp stove, turning the chicken pieces with a fork while her dad gathered firewood down the trail. He had put her in charge of supper, which meant she was supposed to supervise the whole meal, and so far nothing had burned. That felt like a victory.

Jude and Darien wandered over from the next campsite, drawn by the smell. "You're making that look good," Jude said, hopping onto the picnic table bench. Darien peered into the pot and asked what else they were having.

"Chicken, rice, and a big salad," Alice said. "The lettuce is in the cooler." She lifted the chicken out of the pan and set it on a plate, then reached for the cutting board to chop the lettuce. Her hand stopped halfway. The board was dotted with spots of raw chicken juice, and a small pool had collected in one corner.

She stood there thinking. She couldn't see anything wrong with the board. It looked almost clean, just damp. But she remembered a poster in the school kitchen from last year's cooking unit, red letters and a picture of a knife. The words had come back to her at exactly the wrong moments, usually during math, and now they arrived at the right one. She had copied it into her notebook once, and she could still picture her own handwriting.

"Wait," she said out loud. Jude and Darien both looked up. "If I chop the lettuce on the board the raw chicken touched, the bacteria from the chicken could spread to the salad. It's called cross-contamination." She pulled a clean board from the dish tub, washed it at the pump, and dried it on a towel. The old board went into the wash bin, and she scrubbed her hands afterward, too, just to be thorough.

"That's why my mom uses different colors," Jude said. "Red board for meat, green for vegetables." Darien nodded slowly, like a rule he'd heard a hundred times had finally become real.

When her dad came back with an armload of wood, Alice told him what she'd almost done. He admitted, a bit guiltily, that their old two-board system back home had gone obsolete when one cracked and they never replaced it. "So we've been using one board for everything since March," he said. "I keep meaning to fix that."

Alice served the salad last, from its own board, under its own clean knife. Jude took a second helping and pointed his fork at the pot. "Tomorrow you supervise, and we'll be your assistants."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends, and once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller.
story:
Bennett stood in Charlie's kitchen with his shoes off, back against the doorframe where Charlie's family had marked heights every birthday since kindergarten. The pencil hovered an inch above his last mark from June.

"Stop sucking in your chin," Charlie said. "You're not a turtle."

Bennett held still while Charlie drew the line. When he stepped away, they both stared at it. Three quarters of an inch since summer. Three quarters, in five months.

"That's it?" Bennett said. "Aylan grew like two inches over the summer alone. His mom keeps buying him pants and he keeps ruining them."

Charlie leaned against the counter, chewing a granola bar. "My cousin says it stops eventually. Like, your bones just quit."

"That can't be right. Bones don't just quit." Bennett slid down to sit on the kitchen floor, because thinking went better sitting down. If bones quit growing, there had to be a reason, and if there was a reason, there might be a way to check on it. He pulled out his phone. "Ask it."

"Ask what?"

"How bones know when to stop."

Charlie typed it in, his diligent thumbs working fast, and they read the answer off the small screen together. Bones grew longer at the growth plates, near the ends, and once those plates closed after puberty, a person stopped getting taller.

"Growth plates," Bennett said slowly. "So they're like, doors. And puberty slams them shut."

"Locked," Charlie said, and mimed turning a key.

Bennett scrolled further and found an X-ray image, some kid's wrist, with the plates showing as dark gaps. "Look. You can actually see them. They're right there at the ends." He turned the phone so Charlie could see, and Charlie's reputation for being unimpressed by everything took a hit, because he leaned in close and went, "Whoa."

"So the question," Bennett said, "is whether mine are still open."

"You can't X-ray yourself, man."

"No, but I can do math." He grabbed a napkin and a pen from the junk drawer. His marks on the doorframe went back years, and he was the kind of kid who kept a growth chart in his own bathroom at home too. If he was still growing, even three quarters of an inch, the doors were still open. He started copying down the dates.

"Is this why you've been eating all my granola bars?" Charlie asked.

Bennett paused, mid-calculation. "Partly."

"You could have just said."

"I'm building bones here, Charlie. It's a project." He put the pen between his teeth, took another bar, and got back to the numbers.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: In winter, strawberries sold in cold regions are usually trucked or flown in from warmer places, and the cost of that transport helps make them pricier.
story:
Levi stood in his grandmother's kitchen on a snowy February morning, staring at the grocery list she had written for his birthday cake. Strawberries, it said, underlined twice, because Levi's favorite cake was strawberry, and his grandmother never did things halfway. Then she coughed in the next room, and Levi remembered why he was the one going to the store: her allergy to cold air made her eyes swell and her throat itch, so on bitter days she stayed inside.

At the little grocery near her house, the strawberries sat in a plastic box, shiny and red, priced at almost seven dollars. Seven dollars! In summer, Levi knew, the farm stand by the river sold whole baskets for two. He picked up the box, put it down, and picked it up again. His friend Molly from school had once portrayed a grocery shopper in their class play, haggling over tomatoes, and now Levi wished she were here to help him argue with somebody.

Instead he studied the label. It said the berries came from a country far to the south, where it was warm right now. Levi turned the box over in his hands, thinking. The strawberries in summer grew in fields nearby, so they just rode a short way in a truck. These winter berries had to be trucked or flown in from warmer places, and that long trip must cost money, which had to be part of why they cost so much. He remembered Mr. Farah-Ali, his neighbor, saying once that when something is scarce and people still want it, the price climbs, and when there is plenty, it sinks.

Levi counted his grandmother's ten dollar bill, took the box to the register, and paid. Back at her house, he set the berries on the counter and sliced them himself so she would not have to touch the cold juice. As he slid the first strawberry onto her plate, he said, "Now you get summer in February."

She smiled and popped it into her mouth.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Canada, a federal bill must pass three readings in both the House of Commons and the Senate before it can receive royal assent.
story:
Camille sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with her laptop open to a government website, a granola bar in one hand and a notebook in the other. Her homework was to explain how a bill became a law, and she had picked a real bill about banning single-use plastics to follow. The problem was that the website kept using words like "second reading" and "Senate," and she could not tell how far the bill had actually gotten or how much road was left.

On a video call, Vada leaned toward her own screen. "Just say it goes through the government and becomes a law," Vada said. "That's basically it, right?"

"That's not basically it," Camille said. "Look, I counted the stages on the tracking page. It has to pass three readings in the House of Commons, and then three readings again in the Senate. Six votes total before it can even get royal assent." She circled the numbers in her notebook, one through six, like rungs on a ladder. "This bill just finished its second reading in the House. So I can figure out exactly how many stages are left. Four. That's the part nobody tells you."

Vada looked skeptical, so Camille scrolled back through the bill's history to test her idea. Every line matched: first reading, second reading, then a pause while a committee studied it, then third reading still to come. When Vada insisted that the Senate part probably did not count, Camille pointed at the site's status bar, which showed the House stages checked off and the Senate ones sitting empty. "You can't refute the checklist," she said. "It's right there."

The insight hit her while she was drawing a diagram: the whole thing was like a relay race with two runners, the House handing off to the Senate, and royal assent as the finish line. If either runner dropped the baton, the bill died and they had to start over. She wrote that at the top of her page, then checked the calendar. The site said the third reading was scheduled for next month, which meant she could actually watch the next stage happen in real time, like tracking a package.

"Is watching a bill even a real thing to do for fun?" Vada asked.

"Way more feasible than my last idea, which was memorizing every MP's name," Camille said. She set her alarm for the morning of the third reading, penciled the date onto the diagram, and drew a small crown next to the finish line. "When it gets royal assent, I'm coloring the whole page gold."

fact: In Westminster-style legislatures such as Canada's and the United Kingdom's, first reading introduces a bill and has it printed without debate.
story:
Simon had watched the legislature on TV for forty minutes waiting for the big speech about the new bill, and nothing happened. A clerk read the bill's title, the Speaker said a few words, and then everyone moved on. Simon slumped on the couch. "They forgot the debate," he told his dad, who just said the class field trip to the town hall meeting on Saturday might help him figure it out.

At the town hall, Ms. Sow had set up a long table with folders, one for every student. "You each get to move a bill through our model legislature," she said. "Simon, you're first." Simon stood up, gripped his folder, and launched into a speech about his bill to make the skating rink free on Saturdays, listing all the reasons it was fair and how much family income it would save. He talked for two full minutes before Ms. Sow raised her hand.

"That's not what happens at this stage," said Vera from the second row. "Watch." She stood, held up her own bill about fixing the cracked basketball court, and said only, "I move that this bill be introduced and printed." Then she sat down. Simon blinked. "That's it?" he asked. "That's it," Vera said. "It's called first reading. No debate yet. The bill gets introduced and printed so everyone can read it before they argue about it later."

Simon thought back to the TV. No wonder there was no speech. It was the first reading, and the debate came after, once the printed bill was in everyone's hands. He tried again, word for word: "I move that Bill Twelve be introduced and printed." Ms. Sow stamped his folder, and Sophia whispered, "See? Shortest speech ever, and it still counts." Simon grinned and slid the folder down the table to be copied for every member.
